author: श्रीमदानन्दतीर्थभगवत्पादाचार्य
commentary:
स्थिता प्रज्ञा= ज्ञानं यस्य स स्थितप्रज्ञः । भाष्यतेऽनयेति भाषा, लक्षणमित्यर्थः । उक्तं लक्षणम् अनुवदति लक्षणान्तरं पृच्छामीति ज्ञापयितुम् - समाधिस्थस्येति ॥ 

कम्= ब्रह्माणम्, ईशम्= रुद्रं च वर्तयतीति केशवः । तथाहि निरुक्तिः कृता हरिवंशेषु रुद्रेण कैलासयात्रायाम् । 
 ‘हिरण्यगर्भः कः प्रोक्त ईशः शङ्कर एव च । सृष्ट्यादिना वर्तयति तौ यतः केशवो भवान् ॥’ इति वचनान्तराच्च । 

 किमासीत ? किं प्रत्यासीत ? न चार्जुनो न जानाति तल्लक्षणादिकम् - ‘जानन्ति पूर्वराजानो देवर्षयस्तथैव हि । 
 तथाऽपि धर्मान् पृच्छन्ति वार्तायै गुह्यवित्तये । 
 न ते गुह्याः प्रतीयन्ते पुराणेष्वल्पबुद्धिनाम् ॥’ इति वचनात् ॥५४ ॥
translation:
Acharya Madhva uses this text to uncover the deep etymological roots of key words like Sthitaprajña and Keshava, while addressing a fascinating question: If Arjuna was already a great, enlightened soul, why was he asking questions he likely already knew the answers to?

One whose Prajñā—meaning spiritual wisdom or realization—has become perfectly Sthitā (steady, unshakeable, and anchored) is called a Sthitaprajña.

The word Bhāṣā literally means 'that by which something is described or spoken of.' Therefore, in this context, Bhāṣā means Lakṣaṇam (the defining characteristics, symptoms, or traits).By using the word Samādhisthasya (of one situated in deep meditation), Arjuna is restating the characteristics Krishna just mentioned, in order to signal: 'I am now asking for even further, specific behavioral symptoms of such a soul.'

Acharya Madhva provides the definitive inner etymology of the name Keshava: 'Kam' refers to Chaturmukha Brahma (the creator). 'Īśam' refers to Lord Rudra/Shiva (the destroyer). The one who commands, controls, and directs (vartayati) both of them is called Keśava (the Supreme Lord Vishnu/Krishna). This exact etymological definition (nirukti) was spoken by Lord Rudra (Shiva) himself to Lord Krishna during the Kailasa Yatra section of the Harivamsa Purana: 'Hiraṇyagarbha (Brahma) is called 'Ka', and Shankara (Shiva) is called 'Īśa'. Because You direct both of them in their cosmic duties of universal creation and destruction, You are known as Keśava.'

Arjuna asks: 'How does he sit? Towards what does he restrain his mind?' One should not think that Arjuna was ignorant and did not already know these spiritual symptoms. For as stated in the ancient scriptures: 'The great kings of old and the celestial sages (like Narada) already know these truths perfectly. Yet, they still ask questions about righteousness for the sake of public conversation (vārtāyai) and to reveal hidden spiritual secrets (guhya-vittaye). Without such questions, these deep secrets would never be understood from the Puranas by ordinary people with limited intelligence.'
